lesson.grammar_point: verb + to-infinitive vs verb + -ing (plan to, agree to / avoid, suggest + -ing)

listenings.text: I run project kickoffs for a living, and I always follow three rules. First, I agree on the scope in the first meeting. If you wait, people start to add things, and the timeline moves. Second, I ask every team to choose one point of contact. Ten people talking to ten people is a mess. One person for each workstream is enough. Third, I write down everyone's expectations. What do you expect to see in thirty days? What do you want to avoid? People often forget what they said in the first meeting, so the notes help a lot later. And one more thing: I suggest keeping the weekly check-in short. Fifteen minutes is enough. If it takes an hour, people stop coming.

My worst project started with a kickoff that nobody planned. The vendor arrived with forty slides, and we never talked about responsibilities. Three months later, a server failed, and both teams said the same thing: that is not our job. We lost two weeks arguing. On my next project, I decided to do it differently. Before the kickoff, I sent a one-page table with every task and the name of the person responsible. In the meeting, we only discussed the table, line by line. It took forty minutes. Since then, I always finish a kickoff with one question: is there any task without a name? If the answer is yes, we are not ready to start.
